assets.prompt:
Create a complete 15-second live-action theatrical science-fiction horror scene with four clearly different shots joined by hard cuts. A dangerous incident begins, a human makes a brave decision, and the survivors escape before the scene ends. Enormous practical industrial spaceship sets, thirty adult technicians, a terrifying original creature, physical stunts, heavy machinery, smoke and sparks: the scale and production design of a major feature film. Realistic 35mm texture, anamorphic lens character without black bars, cold blue work lights and hard red emergency light, deep but readable shadows. One consistent lead in every shot: an adult female chief engineer aged 40, close-cropped black hair, dark green utility coveralls, an orange shoulder harness, soot on her left cheek, no helmet. The creature is a massive six-limbed pale armored insectoid with an angular skull, a unique original design. Keep this one location and these identities continuous.

SHOT 1, 0-3.5s: a fast descending crane wide shot reveals an immense spaceship cargo bay, three levels of gantries, dangling chains and thirty technicians running toward a raised steel blast door on frame right. A section of ceiling grating bursts downward and the enormous creature drops heavily onto a cargo container behind them. Its impact buckles the container and throws sparks. Establish the door on the right and the creature pursuing from the left.

HARD CUT. SHOT 2, 3.5-6.5s: chest-height tracking medium close-up moving backward in front of the chief engineer as she turns to face the threat and shoulders a bulky industrial flame projector. Behind her, the last technicians hurry through the open door. She looks at them and shouts one clear English line, "Get behind me!" Her lips match only her own voice. Fear becoming determination is visible in her face.

HARD CUT. SHOT 3, 6.5-11.5s: a wide side-on action shot preserves the same geography. The chief sends one powerful horizontal burst of orange flame toward the creature, driving it back. She immediately retreats through the doorway after her crew. The huge solid steel blast door drops between them and the recoiling creature, landing with a deep crash. Both the escape and the door closing must be fully visible.

HARD CUT. SHOT 4, 11.5-15s: on the SAFE side of the closed door, a tight medium shot of the engineer and several breathless crew members. One final heavy impact dents the solid door behind them without opening it. She lowers the flame projector, exhales and says quietly, "We're clear." The crew's shoulders relax. Hold that resolved human reaction to the end; no new threat, no cliffhanger.

Sound: screaming metal at the opening, running boots and urgent crowd movement, creature roar, a single forceful flame burst, the massive door slam, then breathing and the two assigned dialogue lines. A restrained low cinematic tension pulse may support the action but never cover the dialogue. Physical weight, stable anatomy, natural faces, coherent spatial continuity, decisive editorial cuts. Opaque steel and painted surfaces; no mirrors, reflective glass, transparent visors, holograms or water. No on-screen text, captions, logos, famous actors, gore, comic-book styling or slow motion. This must feel like an actual completed action scene, not a trailer montage or a still image with a camera move.

Create one complete 15-second live-action historical epic scene in four hard-cut shots. A towering siege machine threatens an ancient city, a defender takes one decisive shot, and the machine falls before it can reach the wall. Monumental stone fortifications, an army of two hundred moving adult soldiers, ranks of shields, banners, smoke, dust and a giant practical wooden siege tower. This is large-scale theatrical cinema with tangible extras, detailed costumes and physical destruction. Original characters in a fictional ancient Mediterranean city, no named franchise or recognizable actors. Warm late-afternoon sun, ochre dust, weathered bronze, dark crimson cloth, rich cinematic contrast, 35mm grain, realistic dramatic scale. No black bars.

One consistent hero: an adult woman commander around 35, dark hair tightly braided back, battered matte bronze cuirass, a short dark crimson cloak, a small white cloth band tied around her left upper arm. She has a powerful recurve bow. Her supporting defenders have weathered rectangular shields and practical linen armor. Keep her costume, face, bow and the city geography identical across shots.

SHOT 1, 0-3.5s: an imposing wide crane shot moves along the crowded city battlements. Below, two hundred attackers advance across a dry battlefield while an enormous timber siege tower rolls toward the wall. The tower fills the background and its assault bridge begins to lower. Defenders recoil; the commander's crimson cloak provides a clear foreground silhouette. Establish exposed black pitch-soaked bundles around the tower's wooden base and an empty defensive ditch between tower and wall. The threat must be immediately readable.

HARD CUT. SHOT 2, 3.5-7s: a dynamic medium close-up beside the commander on the battlement. With soldiers moving urgently behind her, she pulls back a flaming arrow, eyes fixed on the tower base. She shouts in English, "For the city!" and releases. Show one clean believable bow release, one arrow only, then her intent reaction. Her visible mouth speaks the line; no voice-over.

HARD CUT. SHOT 3, 7-11.5s: a low wide shot near the massive tower base. The single flaming arrow strikes the exposed pitch bundles. Fire runs rapidly up the oil-dark timber braces, sparks shower outward, and the burning base gives way. The enormous tower visibly leans AWAY from the city wall toward the empty ditch. Background attackers retreat sideways from its path. Convincing heavy timber breakage, dust and cascading debris; readable cause and effect rather than a random explosion.

HARD CUT. SHOT 4, 11.5-15s: a triumphant wide shot from behind the commander and the crowded defenders on the intact battlement. The burning tower finishes collapsing into the ditch below, short of the wall. The threat has been stopped. Dozens of defenders lift their shields and erupt in a spontaneous cheer; the commander lowers her bow and breathes out in relief. Hold the victorious image and complete collapse before the clip ends.

Audio: marching feet, distant battle shouts and wooden wheels, the commander's single assigned line, the taut bow snap, fire roaring, massive timber cracking, then an overwhelming human cheer. Original low orchestral percussion may swell after the collapse; dialogue stays intelligible. No gore, no close-up injuries. Four legible shots at real speed, coordinated background action, coherent direction of movement, strong facial acting. Opaque stone, wood and worn metal; no mirrors, transparent objects, shiny reflections or water. No captions, titles, logos or subtitles. A complete dramatic event with a beginning and a victorious end, not disconnected shots from a trailer.

Create a self-contained 15-second live-action urban disaster rescue scene with four precisely staged shots and hard cuts. An earthquake is destroying an elevated highway. A crowded yellow city bus must clear one widening break to reach the intact exit ramp. It makes the jump, lands safely, and the passengers react with relief before the end. The huge scale of a theatrical disaster blockbuster: dense city skyline, collapsing concrete, distant evacuation crowds, emergency vehicles, dust clouds and forty adult passengers in the bus. Photorealistic physical stunt and heavy vehicle momentum, convincing practical debris augmented by large-scale visual effects. Crisp daylight through dry golden dust, charcoal concrete, a vivid worn yellow bus, dramatic but readable exposure, 35mm cinema texture. No black bars.

Maintain the same bus and lead throughout: an adult female bus driver around 45, short dark curls, navy uniform shirt with sleeves rolled, a yellow woven wristband on her right wrist. The forty passengers are ordinary adults in everyday clothes; their visible reactions and movements are natural. The bus is a full-sized solid yellow city bus with dark opaque side panels and no readable branding. Film the driver directly from INSIDE the cab, never through a windshield or a mirror.

SHOT 1, 0-3.5s: a sweeping wide tracking shot keeps pace with the yellow bus racing from left to right across the elevated highway. Behind it, a long section of bridge folds downward in a chain of cracking concrete spans. Ahead, reveal one short widening gap, about three meters, before the intact exit ramp. Hundreds of distant evacuees and stationary emergency vehicles are safely on the city streets below and away from the collapse. Make the route to safety visually obvious.

HARD CUT. SHOT 2, 3.5-6.5s: an urgent medium close-up from inside the cab, with a glimpse of the crowded aisle behind the driver. She looks straight ahead, grips the wheel, braces herself and shouts in clear English, "Everybody hold on!" The passengers immediately clutch the solid seat backs and lower their heads. She presses forward with determination; no added dialogue or narrator.

HARD CUT. SHOT 3, 6.5-11.5s: a single wide side-on tracking shot clearly shows the bus in its entirety as it clears the short break. The front wheels leave the broken edge, the whole bus travels in a short heavy arc, then all wheels land on the solid exit ramp with a violent believable suspension bounce. Concrete from the former span drops behind its rear wheels. The bus remains intact, stable and pointed forward. Show the takeoff AND the completed landing within this shot. Dust and debris fall downward, never conceal the vehicle or turn the action into a fireball.

HARD CUT. SHOT 4, 11.5-15s: inside the now-safe bus, a medium two-level composition shows the driver in front and relieved passengers down the aisle. Their bodies settle after the landing. One adult passenger lets out a disbelieving laugh, others cheer and embrace; the driver releases a breath and gives a small exhausted smile while continuing to steer. The danger has ended. Hold this emotional payoff until the cut; no new disaster or cliffhanger.

Native sound: the deep rolling earthquake, cracking concrete and roaring engine, one clearly assigned female dialogue line, a brief airy gap before the heavy landing thump, then suspension rattling and human relief. An original restrained urgent score may build under the action and resolve at the landing. Faces, hands, bus size, vehicle direction and costumes stay consistent across the four shots. Real-time momentum, no slow motion, no fantasy physics, no floating debris. No mirrors, glass close-ups, transparent objects, underwater scenes, glossy reflections, graphic injuries, subtitles, titles, logos or famous actors. This is a finished miniature rescue scene with cause, action and payoff, not generic destruction footage.

A polished five-second cinematic caper sequence in a small 1970s cinema projection room, two deliberate shots with one clean hard cut. One original fictional adult male projectionist, about 55, close-cropped grey hair, short grey beard, navy work shirt with rolled sleeves. Matte teal plaster walls, bulky dark painted projection machinery, opaque metal film cans, warm practical tungsten bulbs, subtle 35mm grain and deep burgundy accents. No glass panels, mirrors, transparent props or glossy reflections. SHOT 1, 0-2 seconds: tight low-angle close-up of his hand slamming an empty round film-can lid onto a felt-covered workbench; it lands with a sharp dull clack, he immediately turns toward the doorway. SHOT 2, 2-5 seconds: hard cut to a medium close-up at eye level as he leans toward the doorway, eyebrows raised in urgent disbelief, and says clearly in English, "Where's my ending?" Finish on his expectant look, leaving a clean reaction beat. Small purposeful camera push-in in the second shot. Audio: lid clack, low mechanical hum, one natural male voice with perfectly assigned lips; no music, narrator, subtitles, on-screen words or extra dialogue. Concrete physical action, strong acting, grounded lighting, crisp face and hands.

Animate the provided opening frame as a five-second cinematic caper sequence, keeping the exact woman, short dark curls, ochre cotton jacket, matte dark-blue film canister and backstage cinema corridor. Two purposeful shots with a hard cut, consistent screen direction. SHOT 1, 0-2 seconds: she takes two quick decisive steps toward the burgundy curtain, pulls it aside with her right hand, keeping the canister tight under her left arm; the camera tracks right with her, fabric sweeps past the lens. SHOT 2, 2-5 seconds: cut to a tight three-quarter close-up on her face just beyond the curtain, still looking screen right. She lifts the canister into the lower frame, catches her breath and says in English with a triumphant half-smile, "Found your ending." End on her proud smile, no further speech. Warm tungsten and teal shadows, natural skin, subtle 35mm grain, controlled handheld energy. Audio: quick footsteps, heavy fabric swish, one clear female voice with natural synchronized lips, quiet room tone. No music, subtitles, narrator, extra dialogue, mirrors, glass, transparent objects, glossy reflections or new props.

A five-second cinematic payoff sequence inside the 1970s cinema from @Video1. Use the male projectionist's appearance, navy work shirt, room palette and understated performance from @Video1, and the woman's exact appearance, short dark curly hair, ochre jacket and opaque matte blue film canister from @Image1. This is a new scene, not a replay. Three clean shots, no dissolves. SHOT 1, 0-1.5 seconds: close-up of the woman's two hands sliding the closed canister from screen left onto the felt-covered bench; the man's hand stops it decisively from screen right, one satisfying clack. SHOT 2, 1.5-3.3 seconds: hard cut to the man's close-up as his tension turns into a grin; looking toward her off-screen left he says in English, "Roll it." Only he speaks. SHOT 3, 3.3-5 seconds: hard cut to a medium two-shot, she gives a relieved laugh without words and he reaches to the projector's large opaque switch; the machine starts with a tactile click and accelerating whirr. Finish with both faces readable, looking toward the machinery. Match warm tungsten, matte teal plaster and rich burgundy, subtle analog grain, grounded caper-film realism. All props opaque and matte; no mirrors, glass, transparent parts, projected screen image, overlays, subtitles, music or extra dialogue. Clear physical causality and one action per shot.
